why: In Europe, much of security and privacy work is driven by law: GDPR for personal data, NIS2 for essential and important entities, DORA for banks, insurers and other financial entities. GRC analysts are hired to read these texts, turn them into controls the teams can run, collect the evidence and keep the deadlines. Interviews test whether you know the key articles and timelines, and whether you can explain what they mean on a Monday morning.
outcome: explain the GDPR principles and lawful bases, keep a record of processing, run a DPIA and handle a personal data breach within 72 hours, tell whether NIS2 or DORA applies and what they require, map one control set to several regulations and ISO 27001, and prepare evidence for an inspection.

lessons.title: Why regulations shape GRC work
text: Governance, risk and compliance teams sit between the law and the people who run systems. A regulation is written in general terms: “appropriate technical and organisational measures”, “without undue delay”, “proportionate to the risk”. Engineers cannot run a sentence like that. The GRC analyst’s job is to translate it into a chain: law → requirement → control → evidence. The requirement is what the text asks of your organisation, the control is what a named team does to meet it, and the evidence is what proves the control ran.

Three European texts dominate this work. The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, applying since 25 May 2018) protects personal data and applies to almost every organisation that handles data about people in the EU. NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) raises the cybersecurity level of essential and important entities in critical sectors. DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, applying since 17 January 2025) sets digital operational resilience rules for financial entities. A regulation applies directly in every member state; a directive must first be transposed into national law, which is why NIS2 details can differ from one country to another.

The difference between a requirement and a control matters in interviews. “Notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach within 72 hours” is a requirement. “The DPO decides on notification using the breach assessment form, and every incident tagged ‘personal data’ is sent to the DPO within one hour” is a control. “The breach register shows the time of awareness, the decision and the notification date for each case” is the evidence. An auditor or a regulator will ask for the evidence, not for your intentions.

Regulators also check accountability: the GDPR says the controller must be able to demonstrate compliance (art. 5(2)), NIS2 makes the management body approve and oversee cybersecurity measures, and DORA gives the management body the final responsibility for ICT risk. So GRC work produces documents people sign, registers that are kept current and tests whose results are recorded. If it is not written down and dated, for an inspector it did not happen.

In practice, a GRC analyst spends the week on concrete tasks: updating the record of processing after a new tool is bought, checking a supplier contract for the right clauses, preparing the quarterly compliance report for the risk committee, chasing evidence before an audit, and helping the security team classify an incident against the regulatory thresholds.
points: Law → requirement → control → evidence: every compliance task fits this chain.
A regulation (GDPR, DORA) applies directly; a directive (NIS2) is transposed into national law first.
A control has an owner, a frequency and a trace; evidence proves it ran.
Accountability: you must be able to demonstrate compliance, not only claim it.

example.code:
Law          GDPR art. 33
Requirement  Notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach
             within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach
             is unlikely to result in a risk to people
Control      Breach response procedure: triage, risk assessment,
             DPO decision, notification form, breach register
Owner        DPO (decision), CISO (facts and containment)
Frequency    Every incident involving personal data; yearly exercise
Evidence     Approved procedure, breach register with timestamps,
             last exercise report
Test         Sample 3 incidents: time from awareness to decision
example.note: One requirement, one control, one owner, one trace: the line an auditor can test.

lessons.title: GDPR principles and lawful bases
text: Article 5 of the GDPR sets seven principles that every processing of personal data must respect: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation (data collected for a specified purpose is not reused for an incompatible one); data minimisation (only what is needed); accuracy; storage limitation (kept no longer than necessary); integrity and confidentiality (security); and accountability, the controller’s duty to demonstrate all of the above. Most audit findings trace back to one of them: a database kept forever breaks storage limitation, a form asking for a date of birth it never uses breaks data minimisation.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person: a name, an e-mail address, an employee number, an IP address, a location, a cookie identifier. The controller decides why and how data is processed; the processor processes it on the controller’s behalf (a payroll provider, a cloud CRM). The roles drive the duties, so the first question about any new tool is “who is controller, who is processor?”.

Article 6 lists six lawful bases, and every processing needs one: consent; performance of a contract with the person; compliance with a legal obligation; protection of vital interests; a task carried out in the public interest or official authority; and legitimate interests, when they are not overridden by the person’s rights. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give, which is why it is a poor basis for employee data: employees are rarely free to refuse. Legitimate interests needs a documented balancing test.

Some data is more sensitive. Article 9 covers special categories (health, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, genetic and biometric data used to identify someone, sex life and sexual orientation): processing them is prohibited unless one of the specific exceptions applies, such as explicit consent or obligations in employment law. In interviews, being able to say which base fits which processing, and why consent is not the default answer, is a strong signal.

Fines are the headline: up to 20 million euros or 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, for breaches of the principles, lawful bases or people’s rights; a lower tier (up to 10 million euros or 2 %) covers other duties such as security or records. In France the supervisory authority is the CNIL. Fines are only one tool: authorities also issue orders to bring processing into compliance, and the reputational damage of a public sanction often costs more.
points: Seven principles in art. 5, ending with accountability.
Six lawful bases in art. 6; choose one per purpose and document it.
Consent is not the default; it is weak for employees.
Special categories (art. 9) are prohibited unless an exception applies.
Fines up to 20 M€ or 4 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

                                                            security rules
Delivering customer orders        Contract                  Needed to deliver
Fraud detection on payments       Legitimate interests      Balancing test
                                                            documented
Newsletter to prospects           Consent                   Opt-in, easy
                                                            unsubscribe

                                                            retention

lessons.title: GDPR in operations: records, rights, processors and transfers
text: The record of processing activities (art. 30) is the inventory of what the organisation does with personal data. For a controller, each entry lists at least the controller and DPO contact details, the purposes, the categories of people and of data, the recipients, transfers outside the EU, the planned erasure periods where possible, and a general description of the security measures. Processors keep their own record of the processing they do for clients. There is an exemption for organisations under 250 employees, but it does not apply when the processing is not occasional, is likely to result in a risk, or includes special categories, so in practice most organisations keep one.

A record is only useful if it is current. The GRC analyst ties it to other processes: the purchasing workflow (a new SaaS tool means a new or updated entry), the project intake (a new feature with personal data triggers a privacy review) and the yearly review with each business owner. A good indicator for the compliance report is the share of entries that are complete: lawful basis documented, retention period set, owner named.

People have rights over their data: information (arts. 13–14), access (art. 15), rectification (art. 16), erasure (art. 17), restriction (art. 18), portability (art. 20), objection (art. 21) and rights related to automated decisions (art. 22). The organisation must answer without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests, after telling the person. Operations need a channel, identity checks proportionate to the risk, a log of requests and deadlines, and a way to find the person’s data across systems: the record of processing is the map.

When a processor handles data for you, article 28 requires a contract (often called a DPA, data processing agreement) that covers, among others: processing only on documented instructions, confidentiality of the staff, security measures, conditions for using sub-processors, help with rights requests and breaches, deletion or return of data at the end, and making information available for audits. Checking these clauses is a routine GRC task in supplier onboarding.

Transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area are restricted by Chapter V of the GDPR. They are allowed to countries with an adequacy decision from the European Commission, or with appropriate safeguards such as the standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules, usually with a transfer impact assessment of the destination country’s laws. For an analyst, the practical questions are: where is the data stored and accessed from, which mechanism covers it, and is it written in the contract and the record?
points: Record of processing (art. 30): purposes, people, data, recipients, transfers, retention, security.
Rights requests: answer within one month, extendable by two months.
Art. 28 contract with every processor: instructions, security, sub-processors, audits, end of contract.
Transfers outside the EEA need an adequacy decision or safeguards such as standard contractual clauses.

Controller         Example SAS, HR department; DPO: dpo@example.com
Purpose            Select candidates for open positions
Lawful basis       Pre-contractual steps (art. 6(1)(b))
People             Applicants

Recipients         HR, hiring managers, applicant tracking system

Transfers          None outside the EEA

lessons.title: DPIA and personal data breaches
text: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA, art. 35) is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms. The GDPR names three cases: systematic and extensive evaluation of people, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects; large-scale processing of special categories or criminal data; and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. Supervisory authorities publish lists of processing that need one, and the European guidelines give nine criteria (such as sensitive data, large scale, vulnerable people, innovative technology, matching datasets): meeting two of them usually means a DPIA is needed.

A DPIA describes the processing and its purposes, assesses necessity and proportionality, assesses the risks to people (not to the company: illegitimate access, unwanted change, disappearance of data) and lists the measures that address them. The DPO gives advice, the business owner decides, and if a high residual risk remains the controller must consult the supervisory authority before starting (art. 36). The CNIL publishes a free PIA tool that many French teams use.

A personal data breach is a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. It is not only hacking: an e-mail sent to the wrong recipients, a lost laptop without encryption or a ransomware attack that makes data unavailable are all breaches.

Article 33 requires the controller to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. The clock counts calendar hours, weekends included, and starts when the organisation has a reasonable degree of certainty that a breach affecting personal data happened. If the facts are not all known, notify in phases and complete later; a late notification must give the reasons for the delay. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay. When the risk to people is high, article 34 also requires informing the people concerned, in clear language, without undue delay.

Every breach, notified or not, goes into the internal breach register (art. 33(5)) with the facts, effects and remedial action. This register is one of the first documents an inspector asks for. Typical failures: the security team handles the incident for days before anyone tells the DPO, nobody records the time of awareness, or a breach is judged “low risk” without a written reason.
points: DPIA before high-risk processing (art. 35); two of the nine criteria usually means yes.
High residual risk after the DPIA: prior consultation of the authority (art. 36).
Breach: notify the authority within 72 hours of awareness (art. 33), weekends included.
High risk to people: inform them too (art. 34).
Record every breach in the breach register, even when not notified.

Fri 19:30  Confirmed: 4,200 customer records (names, e-mails,
           phone numbers) sent to an unknown server
           -> awareness: the 72-hour clock starts
Fri 20:00  DPO informed, incident ticket tagged "personal data"

Sat 15:00  Decision: notify the CNIL (risk: phishing of customers)

Mon 19:30  72-hour deadline (Fri 19:30 + 72 h)
Tue        Customers informed? Only if high risk (art. 34)

lessons.title: NIS2: scope, duties and reporting
text: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) replaced the first NIS directive. Member states had to transpose it by 17 October 2024. It covers many more sectors: Annex I lists sectors of high criticality (energy, transport, banking, financial market infrastructures, health, drinking water, waste water, digital infrastructure, ICT service management between businesses, public administration, space), and Annex II other critical sectors (postal and courier services, waste management, chemicals, food, manufacturing of certain products, digital providers such as online marketplaces and search engines, research).

Scope depends on sector and size. As a general rule, medium-sized and large organisations in these sectors are in scope (medium means at least 50 employees, or more than 10 million euros of annual turnover and balance sheet), while some entities are covered whatever their size, such as providers of public electronic communications networks, trust service providers or DNS service providers. In-scope entities are classed as essential (mostly large entities in Annex I sectors) or important. Both have the same security duties; the difference is supervision, proactive for essential entities and after the fact for important ones, and the maximum fines.

Article 21 requires cybersecurity risk-management measures, based on an all-hazards approach, that include at least: risk analysis and security policies; incident handling; business continuity, backup management and crisis management; supply chain security; security in the acquisition, development and maintenance of systems, including vulnerability handling; policies to assess the effectiveness of the measures; basic cyber hygiene and training; cryptography and encryption; human resources security, access control and asset management; and multi-factor authentication where appropriate. Anyone who knows ISO 27001 recognises most of the list.

NIS2 puts the management body in the front line (art. 20): it must approve the risk-management measures, oversee their implementation and can be held liable for failures; its members must follow training. For a GRC analyst this means board-level reporting: a status of the art. 21 measures, the main risks, incidents and the plan, presented and minuted.

Article 23 sets the reporting of significant incidents to the CSIRT or the competent authority: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, an incident notification within 72 hours with an initial assessment, intermediate reports on request, and a final report within one month after the notification. In France the national authority is the ANSSI. The French transposition law was still being finalised after the 2024 deadline, so check the current national text and implementing rules before stating details for France.
points: Directive (EU) 2022/2555, transposition deadline 17 October 2024.
Essential and important entities: same duties, different supervision and fines.
Art. 21: ten areas of risk-management measures, close to ISO 27001.
Management body approves, oversees, can be held liable, and is trained.
Art. 23: early warning 24 h, notification 72 h, final report within one month.

example.code:
NIS2 significant incident: reporting timeline (art. 23)
T0          Entity becomes aware of a significant incident
T0 + 24 h   Early warning to the CSIRT / competent authority
            (suspected malicious act? cross-border impact?)
T0 + 72 h   Incident notification: initial assessment,
            severity, impact, indicators of compromise
On request  Intermediate report on progress
Notification + 1 month
            Final report: detailed description, root cause,
            measures applied, cross-border impact
example.note: If personal data is involved, the GDPR 72-hour notification to the data protection authority runs in parallel.

lessons.title: DORA: the five pillars for financial entities
text: DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) applies since 17 January 2025 to financial entities: banks, payment and e-money institutions, investment firms, insurers and reinsurers, crypto-asset service providers, trading venues, central counterparties and others. Being a regulation, it applies directly, and for these entities its ICT rules take precedence over the corresponding NIS2 duties. It is complemented by technical standards (RTS and ITS) that set the detailed content. In France the supervisors are the ACPR and the AMF.

Pillar 1, ICT risk management: a documented ICT risk management framework, owned by the management body, which has the final responsibility for managing ICT risk. It covers identification of assets and dependencies, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, backup policies, learning from incidents and communication. Proportionality applies: smaller entities have a simplified framework.

Pillar 2, ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting: entities classify incidents with common criteria (clients affected, duration, data losses, critical services, economic impact…) and report major ones to their supervisor in stages. Under the technical standards, the initial notification is due within 4 hours of classifying the incident as major and no later than 24 hours after becoming aware of it, the intermediate report within 72 hours and the final report within one month. Pillar 3, digital operational resilience testing: a testing programme with at least yearly tests of systems supporting critical or important functions, and, for entities designated by their supervisors, threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years.

Pillar 4, ICT third-party risk: a strategy for ICT suppliers, due diligence before contracting, key clauses in contracts (service levels, locations, access and audit rights, exit plans) and a register of information listing all contractual arrangements with ICT third-party service providers, which supervisors collect. Pillar 5, oversight of critical ICT third-party providers: the European Supervisory Authorities designate critical providers (large cloud providers, for example) and a lead overseer supervises them directly. Information sharing on cyber threats between financial entities is also encouraged.

For a GRC analyst in a bank or an insurer, DORA work is very concrete: keeping the register of information complete and consistent, checking that every ICT contract supporting a critical function has the required clauses, maintaining the incident classification grid, planning the testing programme and reporting the status to the management body.
points: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, applies since 17 January 2025, to financial entities.
Five pillars: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, ICT third-party risk, oversight of critical providers.
Management body has the final responsibility for ICT risk.
TLPT at least every three years for designated entities.
Register of information: every contract with an ICT third-party provider.

                                 yearly review by the management body
2 Incident management            Classification grid, major-incident
  and reporting                  reports: initial / intermediate / final
3 Resilience testing             Test plan, yearly tests of critical
                                 systems, TLPT if designated
4 ICT third-party risk           Register of information, contract
                                 clauses, exit plans, due diligence

  ICT providers                  designated critical
example.note: Pillar 5 is run by the supervisors; the entity mainly needs to know which providers it relies on.

lessons.title: One control set for several regulations
text: An organisation subject to GDPR, NIS2 and DORA, and certified ISO 27001, does not run four separate programmes. It runs one control set and maps each control to every requirement it covers. A multi-factor authentication control, for example, supports GDPR art. 32 (security of processing), NIS2 art. 21 (multi-factor authentication), DORA’s ICT risk management and ISO 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.5 (secure authentication). Tested once, its evidence serves all four.

The mapping usually lives in a matrix or a GRC tool: one row per control, with its owner, frequency, evidence and the references it satisfies. The analyst builds it by reading each requirement and asking “which of our controls answers this, fully or partly?”. Gaps appear where a requirement has no control (DORA’s register of information has no ISO 27001 equivalent) or where a control exists but its evidence does not cover the stricter text (an incident procedure that ignores the 24-hour NIS2 early warning).

The strictest rule wins when texts overlap. Incident reporting is the classic example: one incident can require a DORA or NIS2 report to the sector authority and a GDPR notification to the data protection authority, each with its own form and clock. A good incident procedure has a single triage step that asks all the questions at once: is personal data involved, is it a significant (NIS2) or major (DORA) incident, which authorities, which deadlines?

Recurring duties go into a compliance calendar: yearly review of the record of processing, policies reviewed every year, quarterly access reviews, yearly resilience tests, the register of information update, management body training, supplier reviews. Each entry has an owner and a due date, and overdue items are reported. The calendar turns compliance from a project into a routine.

Coverage indicators make the status visible: percentage of controls tested this year, percentage of record entries complete, number of ICT contracts missing required clauses, open findings by age. They feed the risk committee report. Keep the formulas simple and the definitions written down, so the numbers mean the same thing every quarter.
points: One control, several references: test once, reuse the evidence.
Mapping matrix: control, owner, frequency, evidence, references.
Gaps: requirements with no control, or evidence weaker than the strictest text.
One incident triage for every regulator and every clock.
Compliance calendar: every recurring duty with an owner and a due date.

lessons.title: Working with the DPO, legal, the CISO and regulators
text: The data protection officer (DPO, arts. 37–39) is mandatory for public authorities and for organisations whose core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of people on a large scale, or large-scale processing of special categories. The DPO informs and advises, monitors compliance, gives advice on DPIAs and is the contact point for the supervisory authority. The DPO must be involved early, must not receive instructions on how to carry out these tasks and reports to the highest management level. The DPO advises; the business owner remains responsible for the decision.

Legal interprets the texts and drafts contracts; the CISO owns security controls and incident response; the risk and compliance functions own the framework and the reporting. The GRC analyst often connects them: turning the DPO’s advice into a control, checking that the CISO’s evidence matches the regulatory wording, preparing the files legal needs for a contract review. A RACI for the main processes (breach notification, rights requests, supplier onboarding, incident reporting) avoids the classic gap where everyone assumes someone else notified the authority.

Regulators inspect. The CNIL can carry out on-site inspections, online checks, document requests and hearings; NIS2 gives national authorities powers of audits and inspections, stronger for essential entities; DORA supervisors review ICT risk as part of their supervision. An inspection usually starts with a request for documents: record of processing, breach register, DPIAs, processor contracts, policies, incident reports, the latest management body minutes on cybersecurity.

Preparation is an evidence exercise. Keep a ready pack of the key documents with their dates and approvals, know who speaks for which topic, record exactly what was asked and what was given, never improvise an answer on a figure you are not sure of (say you will confirm in writing) and never create or back-date documents during an inspection. After it, track every finding as an action with an owner and a date, like an audit finding.

In interviews, show that you understand the human side: you need the business to answer your questionnaires, the CISO to share incident timestamps and legal to accept a pragmatic reading. Being precise on articles and deadlines earns trust; being able to explain them in plain words to a product manager earns cooperation.
points: DPO: advises and monitors, does not decide; involved early, independent, reports to top management.
RACI for breach notification, rights requests, supplier onboarding and incident reporting.
Inspections start with documents: records, registers, DPIAs, contracts, minutes.
Never improvise or back-date during an inspection; confirm in writing.
Findings become tracked actions with an owner and a date.

[ ] Record of processing activities (art. 30), last review date
[ ] Breach register (art. 33(5)) and the last notifications
[ ] DPIAs for high-risk processing, with DPO advice
[ ] Processor contracts (art. 28) for the main providers
[ ] Information security policy and incident procedure
[ ] NIS2 / DORA incident reports and classification grid

lessons.title: GDPR details interviews check
text: Pseudonymised data, where names are replaced by codes but a key exists somewhere, is still personal data, because the person can be identified again. Only truly anonymous data, where nobody can identify the person any more by reasonable means, is outside the GDPR. Roles matter just as much: the controller decides why and how data is processed, the processor acts only on its documented instructions, and two organisations that decide together are joint controllers and must agree on who does what. A processor that reuses the data for its own purposes becomes a controller for that use.

Consent is valid only if it is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give: no pre-ticked box, no consent buried in general terms. It is rarely valid in employment because of the imbalance of power. Cookies and similar trackers follow an extra rule from the ePrivacy directive (in France, article 82 of the Loi Informatique et Libertés): non-essential cookies such as advertising need prior consent, and refusing must be as easy as accepting. The CNIL has fined large websites for making refusal harder than acceptance.

Data protection by design and by default (article 25) means building the rules into projects and systems from the start: minimal data collected by default, privacy settings on the protective side, pseudonymisation where possible, retention periods applied automatically, access limited by role. Retention is set per purpose; examples commonly used in France are unsuccessful applicants up to 2 years after the last contact, prospects up to 3 years after the last contact, accounting documents 10 years and CCTV footage generally up to one month.

A data protection officer is mandatory for public authorities and for organisations whose core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of people on a large scale, or large-scale processing of special categories or criminal data. The DPO informs and advises, monitors compliance, advises on DPIAs and is the contact point for the authority and for people. The DPO must be independent, involved early, given resources and free from conflicts of interest, which is why the head of IT or of marketing is usually not a suitable DPO.

Transfers to the United States changed twice. In July 2020 the Schrems II judgment of the Court of Justice of the EU invalidated the Privacy Shield and required a transfer impact assessment, with supplementary measures such as encryption with keys kept in the EU, when relying on standard contractual clauses. Since July 2023 the EU-US Data Privacy Framework is an adequacy decision for American companies certified under it: check the official list for the company and the service. Remember that remote access is a transfer too: a support team outside the EU that can view EU customer data is a transfer even if the data is stored in Europe.
points: Pseudonymised data is personal data; only truly anonymous data is outside the GDPR.
Controller decides, processor follows instructions, joint controllers decide together.
Consent: free, specific, informed, unambiguous, easy to withdraw; non-essential cookies need consent and refusing must be as easy as accepting.
Privacy by design and by default (article 25); retention set per purpose and applied in the tools.
Transfers to the US: Schrems II (2020), then the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (2023) for certified companies; remote access is a transfer.

pitfalls: Writing policies that repeat the law without saying who does what, when, and what trace it leaves.
Choosing consent as the lawful basis for everything, including employee data.
Counting the 72 hours in working days: weekends and holidays count.

Keeping a record of processing that was filled in once in 2018 and never updated.
Signing a SaaS contract without the art. 28 clauses, or, for a financial entity, without adding it to the DORA register of information.
Running separate GDPR, NIS2, DORA and ISO projects that test the same control four times with different evidence.

exercises.q: Match each requirement with the text it comes from.
pairs: Early warning to the CSIRT within 24 hours
Register of information on ICT third-party contracts
Cybersecurity risk-management measures approved by the management body
exercises.answer: GDPR covers personal data (records, processors, breaches), NIS2 the cybersecurity of essential and important entities (measures, governance, incident reporting), DORA the digital operational resilience of financial entities (ICT risk, testing, third parties).

exercises.q: Which text is the main one for each situation?

groups.name: GDPR
items: A customer asks for a copy of their data
A new HR tool will process employee health data
An e-mail with 300 candidate CVs went to the wrong address

groups.name: NIS2
items: A large drinking-water company sets up its cybersecurity measures
A hospital must send an early warning to the CSIRT after a ransomware attack

groups.name: DORA
items: An insurer lists all its ICT supplier contracts for its supervisor
A bank designated by its supervisor plans a threat-led penetration test

exercises.answer: Personal data and people’s rights point to the GDPR; cybersecurity duties of entities in critical sectors (water, health) to NIS2; ICT resilience of financial entities to DORA. Several texts can apply at once: the hospital’s ransomware attack is probably also a personal data breach.

exercises.q: Put the personal data breach response in order.
steps: Detect the incident and contain it
Confirm personal data is affected and record the time of awareness
Inform the DPO and assess the risk to people
Decide on notification and notify the authority within 72 hours if required
Inform the people concerned if the risk is high
Record the breach, its effects and the actions in the breach register
exercises.answer: Contain first, then establish the facts and the time of awareness (it starts the 72-hour clock), assess the risk with the DPO, notify the authority (art. 33), inform the people if the risk is high (art. 34), and record everything in the breach register (art. 33(5)), notified or not.

exercises.q: In E3, the day of the GDPR notification deadline: the detection day plus the hours allowed, counted in whole days (the hour of the day stays in column C).
exercises.hint: Add the hours to the detection hour, divide by 24 and keep the whole days with INT, then add them to the detection day.
exercises.explain: (21 + 72) / 24 = 3.875, so INT gives 3 whole days: 14 + 3 = day 17, and MOD(C3+D3,24) gives the hour, 21:00. Detected on Friday the 14th at 21:00, the deadline is Monday the 17th at 21:00: calendar hours, weekend included.

exercises.q: In F2, how many hours are left before the 72-hour deadline at the time of the check (day and hour in D2 and E2)?
exercises.hint: Turn each moment into hours (day × 24 + hour); the deadline is the awareness moment plus the hours allowed in B3.
exercises.explain: Awareness = 14 × 24 + 19 = 355 h; deadline = 355 + 72 = 427 h; check = 16 × 24 + 9 = 393 h; 427 − 393 = 34 hours left. Converting everything into one unit (hours) avoids mistakes when the deadline crosses midnight or a weekend.

exercises.q: In E3, the maximum GDPR fine for company Beta under the higher tier: the fixed cap or the share of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
exercises.hint: Whichever is higher = MAX of the fixed cap and turnover × 4 %.
exercises.explain: 4 % of 2,000,000,000 = 80,000,000, higher than 20,000,000, so the cap is 80 M€. For Alpha, 4 % of 300 M€ is 12 M€, so the 20 M€ fixed cap applies. These are maximums: the actual fine depends on the gravity, duration, cooperation and other factors of art. 83.

exercises.q: In E8, the share of record of processing entries that are complete: lawful basis documented (Yes) and a retention period set (more than 0 months).
exercises.hint: COUNTIFS with two criteria (Yes, >0) divided by the number of entries (COUNTA of the names).
exercises.explain: Payroll, Recruitment and Customer orders meet both criteria: 3 / 6 = 0.5, so 50 % complete. Written down as a definition, this indicator can be tracked every quarter in the compliance report.

exercises.q: A breach is found on Friday evening. What do you do?

steps.text: Friday 19:30: the SOC confirms that 4,200 customer records (names, e-mails, phone numbers) were exported to an unknown server. The DPO is off until Monday. What now?

choices.label: Record 19:30 as the time of awareness, contain, and reach the DPO or their deputy tonight
choices.feedback: The 72-hour clock has started and counts the weekend. The procedure must name a deputy who can be reached.

choices.label: Contain, and wait for the DPO on Monday morning to decide
choices.feedback: By Monday morning 60 of the 72 hours are gone, and nobody has assessed the risk to customers.

choices.label: Wait until the investigation is finished before calling it a breach
choices.feedback: Awareness is a reasonable degree of certainty, not a finished investigation. You can notify in phases.

steps.text: Saturday: the scope is confirmed, the data could be used for phishing, but the root cause is still unknown. Notify the CNIL?

choices.label: Yes, send an initial notification now and complete it when the facts are known
choices.feedback: Phased notification is allowed: send what you know within 72 hours and add the rest later.

choices.label: No, wait for the root cause so the notification is complete
choices.feedback: A late notification must justify the delay; incomplete facts are not a reason to wait.

steps.text: Do you also need to inform the 4,200 customers?

choices.label: Assess whether the risk to them is high; if so, inform them clearly with advice about phishing
choices.feedback: Art. 34 applies when the risk is high; the decision and its reason go into the breach register either way.

choices.label: Never: notifying the authority is enough
choices.feedback: When the risk to people is high, art. 34 requires informing them too.

exercises.answer: Record the time of awareness, contain, involve the DPO or deputy at once, notify the authority within 72 hours (in phases if needed), inform people if the risk is high, and record everything in the breach register.

exercises.q: A company relies on legitimate interests to process data. What must it have done?
options: Collected explicit consent from each person
Documented a balancing test showing its interest is not overridden by the people’s rights
exercises.answer: Legitimate interests (art. 6(1)(f)) requires weighing the organisation’s interest against people’s rights and expectations, and documenting it (accountability). No prior approval is needed, and consent is a different lawful basis.

exercises.q: A bank is in scope of both NIS2 and DORA for its ICT risk management. Which statement is right?
options: It must apply both texts fully and report every incident twice to the same supervisor
DORA’s rules take precedence for its ICT risk management and incident reporting
NIS2 applies because it is more recent
Neither applies because banks are covered by the GDPR
exercises.answer: DORA is the sector-specific law for financial entities: for the matters it covers, its provisions take precedence over the corresponding NIS2 duties. The GDPR still applies to personal data, so a breach can mean a DORA report and a GDPR notification.

exercises.q: Within how many hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach must the controller notify the supervisory authority, where feasible?
exercises.answer: 72 hours (GDPR art. 33), calendar hours, weekends included. The NIS2 incident notification also uses 72 hours, after a 24-hour early warning.

exercises.q: Pick one requirement, NIS2 art. 21 “supply chain security”, and map it to controls and evidence an auditor could test.
exercises.answer: Requirement: address the security of relationships with direct suppliers and service providers. Controls: 1) supplier inventory with a criticality rating, owner: procurement + security, reviewed yearly; 2) security due diligence before contracting (questionnaire, certifications such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2 reports) for critical suppliers; 3) contract clauses: security requirements, incident notification to us within a set time, audit rights, sub-contracting conditions, exit (and art. 28 clauses when personal data is processed); 4) yearly review of critical suppliers and follow-up of their findings. Evidence: the inventory with dates, completed questionnaires and their assessment, signed contracts with the clauses, review minutes and action tracking. Mapping: also ISO 27001 A.5.19–A.5.21, GDPR art. 28 and, for a financial entity, DORA arts. 28–30 and the register of information. Test: sample 5 critical suppliers and check each has a due diligence, the clauses and a review this year.

exercises.q: A company uses a cloud HR tool to manage its staff. The tool provider only processes the data to run the service, following the company’s settings. What is the provider?
exercises.answer: The company decides why and how the HR data is processed: it is the controller. The provider acts on its instructions: it is a processor, and an article 28 contract is required. If the provider reused the data for its own purposes, such as training a product for other clients, it would become a controller for that use.

exercises.q: A project team wants to deploy a tool that scores employees’ productivity from their computer activity, with automatic alerts to managers. Does it need a DPIA?
options: No, employee data is never sensitive
No, a DPIA is only for health data
Yes: it meets several criteria (evaluation or scoring, systematic monitoring, vulnerable people as employees, possibly innovative technology)
Only if employees give their consent
exercises.answer: Scoring, systematic monitoring and vulnerable people (employees, given the imbalance of power) are three of the nine criteria, so a DPIA is required before deployment, with the DPO consulted and staff representatives informed. The assessment may well conclude that such monitoring is disproportionate. Consent would not fix this, since it is rarely free in employment.

exercises.q: A marketing manager wants to buy a list of 50,000 consumer e-mail addresses to send promotions. What do you advise?
exercises.answer: In France and most of the EU, sending marketing e-mails to consumers requires their prior consent, given to us or to a partner for named partners, unless they are existing customers receiving offers for similar products. A purchased list rarely meets this: I would ask the seller for proof of consent for each address (when, how, which wording, naming our company or a clearly defined category of partners) and the date of collection. Without proof, I advise against it: the risk is CNIL sanctions, complaints and harm to our sender reputation. I would propose alternatives: our own opt-in campaigns, partnerships where the partner sends the offer to its consenting customers, and offers to existing customers with an easy opt-out.

exercises.q: Your company plans to use an American AI service to summarise customer support tickets, which contain names, e-mails and sometimes order problems. What do you check?
exercises.answer: First the roles and the purpose: the service should be a processor acting on our instructions, with an article 28 data processing agreement that forbids using our data to train its models for others. Then the transfer: is the provider certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for this service, or do we need SCCs with a transfer impact assessment, and can we choose EU hosting? Then minimisation: can we remove or pseudonymise names and e-mails before sending tickets, and limit the fields? Then security and retention at the provider: encryption, access, how long prompts and outputs are kept, deletion. I would check whether a DPIA is needed (innovative technology plus large scale may meet two criteria), update the record of processing and the privacy notice, and consult the DPO before launch.

interview.q: What is the difference between a controller and a processor, and why does it matter?
interview.a: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed; the processor processes it on the controller’s behalf and on its instructions, like a payroll provider or a cloud CRM. The roles set the duties: the controller chooses the lawful basis, answers rights requests and notifies breaches; the processor must follow instructions, secure the data, help the controller and tell it about breaches without undue delay. Their relationship needs an art. 28 contract. Getting the roles wrong means missing contracts and unclear responsibilities when something goes wrong.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when a personal data breach is detected.
interview.a: Contain it and establish the facts quickly, and record the time we became reasonably sure personal data was affected, because that starts the 72-hour clock, weekends included. Inform the DPO at once, assess the risk to the people (type and volume of data, identifiability, consequences such as phishing or fraud). If it is not unlikely to result in a risk, notify the authority within 72 hours, in phases if facts are missing; if the risk is high, inform the people too. In parallel check other duties: NIS2 or DORA reporting, contractual notice to clients. Record everything in the breach register, then follow up the root cause and the actions.

Before processing likely to result in a high risk to people. The GDPR names profiling with significant effects, large-scale special categories and large-scale monitoring of public areas; authorities publish lists, and the European guidelines give nine criteria such as sensitive data, large scale, vulnerable people, new technology or combining datasets, where two usually means a DPIA. It describes the processing, checks necessity and proportionality, assesses the risks to people and the measures. The DPO advises, the business decides, and a high residual risk means consulting the authority before starting.

interview.q: How do you know whether NIS2 applies to an organisation?
interview.a: Check the sector first against Annexes I and II (energy, transport, health, digital infrastructure, manufacturing, digital providers…), then the size: generally medium and large organisations, with some entities covered whatever their size. Then classify as essential or important, which changes supervision and fines but not the core duties. Finally, read the national transposition, because the directive is implemented by each member state and the details, the authority and the registration process are national; in France the authority is the ANSSI.

interview.q: What are the five pillars of DORA?
interview.a: ICT risk management, with a framework owned by the management body; ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting of major incidents to the supervisor; digital operational resilience testing, with threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for designated entities; ICT third-party risk management, including contract clauses, exit plans and the register of information; and the oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers, run by the European Supervisory Authorities. It applies since 17 January 2025 to financial entities.

interview.q: We are ISO 27001 certified. Are we compliant with NIS2?
interview.a: Not automatically, but it is a strong start. Most of NIS2 art. 21 maps to ISO 27001 controls: incident handling, continuity, supplier security, access control, cryptography, training. The gaps are usually the scope (the certificate may not cover all the services in scope of NIS2), the reporting timelines of art. 23 with the 24-hour early warning, the management body’s duties (approval, oversight, training) and registration with the authority. I would map each NIS2 requirement to our controls, mark full, partial or missing, and plan the gaps.

interview.q: How would you turn a new regulation into something the teams can run?
interview.a: Break it into requirements, one sentence each, with the article. For each, find the existing control that covers it, or design one with an owner, a frequency and the evidence it produces. Record that in a mapping matrix, reusing controls already tested for ISO 27001 or other texts. Put recurring duties in the compliance calendar, define a few coverage indicators, agree a RACI with the DPO, legal and the CISO, and report the gaps and the plan to management. Then test: sample the evidence as an auditor would.
